note_on_method: This is a state page, so almost everything on it is a claim about coverage rather than about a court. Where it describes a place, the source is that operator's own publication. Where it describes what is missing, it names the town we looked at and the reason we declined it, because 'not listed' and 'does not exist' are different things and a reader deserves to know which one they are looking at. Nobody working on this has played on any court in North Carolina.

slots.coverage:
North Carolina has a hundred counties. This page covers one.

Everything verified in the state sits inside Wake County, in three municipalities: Raleigh, with eleven parks and 44 courts; Apex, with five facilities and 21; and Cary, with three parks and 12. Nineteen sites, 77 courts, three operators, all within about twenty miles of each other in the middle of the Research Triangle. That is not a claim about where pickleball is in North Carolina. It is a description of where we have so far found operators who publish what they have.

That is the whole bar, and it is worth being precise about it. A venue publishes here when the organisation that runs it states its own court count in public. Not a listing site's count, not a count we inferred from a photograph or a map, and not a count we derived by measuring things — a number the operator wrote down. The three towns above clear that bar in three different ways. Raleigh Parks publishes a single pickleball page tabulating every outdoor location with its court count and lighting, then states the citywide total in prose: 44 courts at 11 locations. The eleven listed counts add up to exactly 44, so the source agrees with itself, which is a stronger thing than it sounds. Apex publishes a table with a column each for indoor or outdoor, lights and number of courts, and then most venues repeat their own count on their own page — three of its five are stated twice by the same publisher. Cary states nothing centrally and everything locally: each count appears in the features list of the facility's own page and nowhere else.

What that bar excludes is more interesting than what it includes, because the excluded towns are not places without pickleball. They are places whose operators publish a court locator without a court count.

Durham is the clearest case. Durham Parks and Recreation publishes a proper tennis and pickleball page with two tables. The first lists twelve parks with their tennis court counts and a Yes/No column for whether pickleball lines are painted on them. The second is headed Pickleball Court Information and has exactly one row: Piney Wood Park, twelve courts, twelve lighted. So Durham states a count for one venue and a yes-or-no for four others, and a city page here needs three venues with counts. Durham has more pickleball than Cary does. Cary publishes and Durham does not, so Cary is on this page and Durham is not, and if that seems like the wrong answer it is at least an answer with a reason you can check.

Holly Springs is the same shape at smaller scale: four outdoor courts at the North Main Athletic Complex, stated plainly and free to use, plus indoor open play at the W.E. Hunt Center with "up to three nets" available — which is a description of equipment rather than a count of courts. One countable venue where three are needed.

Wake Forest is the hardest one to leave out, because its numbers are excellent. The town states that pickleball began there in 2009 on one chalked tennis court, that it has installed 32 courts since 2013, and that it currently offers 18 active courts across named facilities: three shared-use indoor at Flaherty Park Community Center, three shared-use indoor at Joyner Park Community Center, eight shared-use outdoor at Flaherty Park Tennis Courts, and four dedicated outdoor at Flaherty Park. Those four figures sum to exactly 18. It is the second-best-documented town we have read in this state. But three of its four entries are at Flaherty Park, so treating them as three separate venues in order to clear a three-venue threshold would be meeting the letter of the rule by breaking its point. Honestly counted, Wake Forest has pickleball at two sites, and two is not three.

And then there is everywhere we have not looked. Charlotte, Greensboro, Winston-Salem, Fayetteville, Wilmington, Asheville, Chapel Hill, Concord, Gastonia, High Point — none of them has been assessed. Their absence from this page carries no information at all about their courts. It is a statement about our reading list.
slots.seasonality:
The honest headline is that we cannot tell you much about North Carolina weather from a source, and we are not going to tell you about it from memory.

What operators do publish, and publish well, is the two things that actually determine whether a court is usable outside a summer afternoon: whether it is lit, and whether there is anywhere indoors to go. On both, the picture across the nineteen verified sites is unusually clear, and on both it is worse than the raw court count suggests.

Start with light, because it decides the working week. Of Raleigh's eleven locations, nine are lit and the city says its outdoor court lighting runs on a timer until 10 p.m.; Fred Fletcher Park and Southgate Park are marked unlit and are therefore daylight-only. Of Apex's five, four are lit and three of those run 6:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. year round. Of Cary's three, exactly one — the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway — is stated as lit; the other two say nothing either way, which we record as unverified rather than as unlit, because an unmentioned light and an absent light are different facts.

Now the part that matters. The single biggest pickleball site in Apex is Pleasant Park, with six courts, and it is the one unlit site in that town. Its published court hours are "Sunrise to 30 minutes after Sunset". So from roughly November to February the largest concentration of courts in Apex shuts in the middle of the afternoon while the smaller lit sites at Kelly Road, Apex Community Park and Seymour run for another six hours. If you plan a winter evening around court count, you will drive to the wrong park. That inversion is the most useful seasonal fact this page can give you, and it comes entirely from two published lines: a No in a Lights column and a sentence about sunset.

Indoors, the state is close to bare — verifiably, rather than actually. There are exactly four verified indoor pickleball courts in North Carolina on this site, all of them at the John M. Brown Community Center in Apex, and they are restricted to players aged 55 and over during designated open gym hours. That is not because indoor pickleball is rare in the Triangle. It is because indoor programmes are published as programmes rather than as facilities. Raleigh Parks runs indoor open play at thirteen community centres, prices it at $3 a session or $15 for a four-month pass, provides nets and balls and keeps paddles to borrow — and publishes no court count for any of the thirteen gyms. Cary rents three indoor courts in the South Gym at Middle Creek Community Center at $10 an hour per court, on a timetable that changes with the season: Thursday and Friday afternoons and Saturday lunchtimes from March to October, shorter hours from November to February. That seasonal timetable is real published evidence that indoor demand shifts with the weather here. Cary publishes no street address for the building, so the venue does not publish, but the timetable still tells you something true about the state.

So: what we can source about seasonality in North Carolina is that the operators themselves treat winter as a different problem. They run indoor sessions on winter schedules, they light most outdoor courts to 10 p.m., and one of them has built its largest site without lights at all. What we cannot source, and will not invent, is anything about summer heat, humidity, thunderstorm closures, or what any of these surfaces is like in August. No North Carolina operator we have read publishes a weather closure policy for a pickleball court, and until one does, that section of this page stays empty on purpose.
slots.notable:
A directory that lists everything equally is not much use, so here is what is genuinely distinctive in the verified North Carolina set — including one venue that is notable precisely because it is missing.

Sanderford Road Park in south-east Raleigh is the largest verified pickleball site in the state: ten permanent courts, all lit. That is nearly a quarter of Raleigh's 44 courts on one site, and more than the whole of Cary's verified provision. It is one of only three Raleigh locations the city describes as permanent pickleball courts rather than lines painted over tennis, and the park page says court reservations are available there — so unlike Method and North Hills it can be booked, which cuts both ways depending on whether you did the booking.

The John M. Brown Community Center in Apex holds the only verified indoor pickleball courts in North Carolina, and at the time of writing the only ones anywhere in this directory. Four of them, on the Town Hall campus at 53 Hunter Street, marked Indoor and lit in the town's own table. The restriction is the whole story: they are available only for ages 55 and over, during designated open gym hours, with a separate Senior 55+ Indoor Pickleball Calendar published for the schedule. If you are under 55 this is not a venue, it is a fact about the state.

Pleasant Park in Apex does something no other operator in this directory does: it publishes live court occupancy. You can look at whether its six pickleball courts are busy before you get in the car. Given that the same park has no lights and closes thirty minutes after sunset, the combination is oddly characteristic of this state's provision — genuinely modern in one respect and plainly limited in another.

Baileywick Park in north Raleigh is the only place in the verified set with covered courts. Its own page lists Court A as covered and Court B as covered centre, and schedules pickleball on Courts A and B, so some of Raleigh's outdoor pickleball is played under a roof. Two cautions travel with that. Court A was closed for repairs when we last checked, with no reopening date published, which is half the pickleball surface at that park. And Baileywick is the venue where Raleigh's own two inventories disagree: the pickleball page says six courts, the city's GIS court layer holds polygons totalling four. We publish six and have flagged it, which is a longer way of saying we do not actually know.

McCrimmon Park in Cary is worth a paragraph for a rule that reads backwards. Its features list puts "Lighted Tennis Court: Reservable 16 hours in advance" directly above "Lighted Pickleball Courts: Non-reservable, first-come, first-served". So at that park the racquet sport you can book is tennis, and the one you cannot book is pickleball — which is better for a player turning up alone, because nobody can have taken the courts before you arrived. It is the largest pickleball site in Cary at six courts.

And the notable absence: Cary Tennis Park. The town states it has four lighted pickleball courts. It is the best-known racquet facility in the county, it has 32 championship tennis courts including seven covered ones, and it hosts the Professional Pickleball Association tour. It does not appear anywhere on this site, because across its facility page, its pickleball page and its court reservations page the Town of Cary prints no street address for it, and a venue does not get a page here without one. That rule costs us the most famous pickleball venue in North Carolina, which is the point of having it: a rule you suspend when it is expensive is not a rule.
slots.growth:
North Carolina is a good place to watch pickleball provision change, because one town has published its own history in enough detail to read the pattern — including the parts most operators quietly leave out.

Wake Forest has published a dated timeline of how the sport arrived and what it displaced. It begins in 2009 with pickleball played on one chalked tennis court. In 2013 a group of citizens approached the town asking for space, initially asking only that lines be taped on a gym floor. In 2014 the town resurfaced the Flaherty Park tennis courts and added eight pickleball courts to them for shared use, and installed four courts at Wake Forest Middle School. In 2015 it resurfaced the tennis courts at Heritage High School and installed six shared-use pickleball courts, and partnered with Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary for temporary courts in a gymnasium. In 2016 it replaced the gym floor at Flaherty Park Community Center and added three courts to it. In 2017 it opened the Flaherty Park Pickleball Courts — four outdoor, lighted, and dedicated, the first courts in the town built for the game rather than borrowed from another one. In 2019 it added three more at the new Joyner Park Community Center. In 2021 it was approached about building a pickleball complex, and in 2022 a $24.4 million parks and recreation bond referendum passed, including a Multipurpose Sports Complex to house dedicated pickleball courts.

That sequence — tape on a gym floor, then lines on tennis courts, then a small dedicated block, then a bond-funded complex — is the arc every town in this state seems to be somewhere along. But the more valuable part of Wake Forest's timeline is the subtraction. The four courts at Wake Forest Middle School are, in the town's own words, no longer in use. The six at Heritage High School were removed once the dedicated courts were installed. The town states it has installed 32 courts since 2013 and currently offers 18 active ones, which means roughly nine of every seventeen courts it has ever built are gone. No directory publishes that. Court counts on listing sites only ever go up, because nobody updates a listing to remove something. A town that tells you what it took away is telling you something about what the shared-use arrangements were actually like to play on.

The same conversion pattern shows in the towns we do publish. In Raleigh, 22 of the 44 outdoor courts are permanent pickleball courts at three sites, and the other 22 are lines painted over tennis at six parks, over basketball at Southgate, and over shared hard courts at Baileywick — an even split between purpose-built and borrowed. In Cary, Ed Yerha Park is the town's designated home of outdoor pickleball and was formerly White Oak Park, renamed for a councilmember who served from 2012 to 2022; the town's own open data still carries the old name on the same map point, which is a small archaeological trace of how recently this provision was reorganised. In Apex, Pleasant Park is the town's newest park and carries its largest block of courts at six.

What is under way right now is smaller and more concrete. Raleigh began a lighting upgrade at North Hills Park on 24 August 2026, closing the courts; daytime play reopened on 2 September and the department targeted 8 September for completion, with night play unavailable until the work finished. Baileywick Park's Pavilion-Court A was closed for repairs on 24 August 2026 with no reopening date published. Apex has playground renovations in the design phase at both Apex Community Park and Kelly Road Park, and its splash pad at Pleasant Park was closed for maintenance — none of which touches a pickleball court, but all of which is the same department's attention and budget.

The honest summary is that North Carolina's public pickleball is roughly half converted tennis and basketball surfaces and half purpose-built courts, that the purpose-built share is growing, that at least one town has a bond-funded complex coming, and that the true statewide court count is a moving number that no source publishes. We can tell you 77 courts across nineteen verified sites in three towns, checked on 3 September 2026. We cannot tell you what North Carolina has, and neither can anyone else who is being careful.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts are there in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Nobody knows, including us, and anyone who gives you a single number for the state is guessing. What we can tell you is that we have verified 77 courts across nineteen sites in three towns — Raleigh, Apex and Cary — where each count was stated by the organisation that runs the courts. North Carolina has a hundred counties and we have verified venues in one of them. The number on this page is a floor with a citation, not an estimate of the total.

faqs.q: Why is everything on this page in one county?
faqs.a: Because that is where we have got to, not because that is where the courts are. Every verified venue is in Wake County — Raleigh, Apex and Cary — which is an artefact of the order we worked in rather than a finding about North Carolina. Raleigh was chosen because its parks department publishes a court count for every location and a citywide total that reconciles with them. Cary and Apex followed partly because they are next door and partly because they publish to the same standard.

faqs.q: Why isn't Durham here? It has more courts than Cary.
faqs.a: It does, and it is not here anyway. Durham Parks and Recreation publishes a Pickleball Court Information table with exactly one row in it: Piney Wood Park, twelve courts, twelve lighted. Its other pickleball is recorded as a Yes in a column on the tennis court table, which tells you lines exist without telling you how many courts they make. A city needs three venues with stated counts to publish here, and Durham states one. That is a gap in what Durham publishes, not in what Durham has.

faqs.q: Where can I play indoors in North Carolina?
faqs.a: There are four verified indoor courts in the state, all at the John M. Brown Community Center in Apex, and they are for players aged 55 and over during designated open gym hours. That is not the whole indoor scene, only the verified part. Raleigh Parks runs indoor open play at thirteen community centres at $3 a session or $15 for a four-month pass with nets and balls provided, and Cary rents three indoor courts at Middle Creek Community Center at $10 an hour. Neither publishes what a venue page needs — Raleigh gives no court count per gym, Cary gives no street address — so neither appears as a venue.

faqs.q: What is the biggest pickleball site in the state?
faqs.a: Of what we have verified, Sanderford Road Park in south-east Raleigh: ten permanent courts, all lit, on one site. Method Community Park, North Hills Park and Baileywick Park in Raleigh, McCrimmon Park in Cary and Pleasant Park in Apex follow with six each. Wake Forest has a larger total than any of those at 18 active courts, but they are spread across facilities we could not honestly count as three separate venues.

faqs.q: Is pickleball still growing in North Carolina?
faqs.a: On the published evidence, yes, and it is changing shape as it grows. The pattern visible in Wake Forest's own timeline — taped lines on a gym floor, then lines painted over tennis courts, then a small block of dedicated courts, then a bond-funded complex — is the arc these towns seem to follow. Wake Forest's 2022 parks bond of $24.4 million includes a Multipurpose Sports Complex for dedicated pickleball. What is less often reported is the subtraction: the same town states it has installed 32 courts since 2013 and has 18 active today, having taken out the courts at Wake Forest Middle School and Heritage High School once dedicated ones existed.

faqs.q: Why is Cary Tennis Park not listed when it hosts professional tournaments?
faqs.a: Because the Town of Cary publishes no street address for it. We read its facility page, its pickleball page and its court reservations page; the town states it has four lighted pickleball courts and 32 championship tennis courts, and prints no address on any of them. A venue does not get a page here without an address, because an address is how a reader finds the place and how we tell two venues apart. It is the most prominent thing this rule has cost us, and suspending the rule for a famous venue would make it not a rule.

faqs.q: How do you decide which North Carolina town to add next?
faqs.a: By whether its operator states its own court counts, for at least three separate sites. Not by population, not by how much pickleball a listing site claims is there. That is why this page covers Apex, population around seventy thousand, and not Charlotte. Towns already assessed and declined are named on this page with the reason, so you can disagree with a specific judgement rather than with a silence.

sources.publisher: City of Raleigh Parks, Recreation and Cultural Resources
sources.evidence: States "Raleigh Parks has 44 outdoor pickleball courts located at 11 locations" and tabulates each location with its court count and lighting; the eleven counts sum to 44. Method Community Park, North Hills Park and Sanderford Road Park are marked as permanent courts (6, 6 and 10); the remaining locations are described as tennis or basketball courts with pickleball lines. Fred Fletcher Park and Southgate Park are marked unlit. "These courts are open from dusk until 10 p.m. with lighting on a timer." Indoor open play runs at thirteen community centres at $3 a session or $15 for a four-month pass, with nets and pickleballs provided and no per-centre court count published.

Pleasant Park's own page gives "Basketball and Pickleball Court Hours: Sunrise to 30 minutes after Sunset" and lists "6 Pickleball courts (view real-time court occupancy)"; Apex Community Park's page states "3 lighted pickleball courts" and hours of 6:30 am - 10:00 pm year round.

sources.publisher: Town of Cary, Parks, Recreation & Cultural Resources
sources.evidence: The Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway lists "Lighted Tennis Court: Reservable 16 hours in advance" directly above "Lighted Pickleball Courts: Non-reservable, first-come, first-served"; the Cary Tennis Park page gives its count as "Six Lighted Tennis Courts and Six Lighted Pickleball Courts" and states Cary Tennis Park itself has "four lighted pickleball courts", 32 championship courts including seven covered, and is hosting the PPA in 2026, without printing a street address on its facility, pickleball or court reservations pages. Ed Yerha Park's page states "Formerly known as White Oak Park, Ed Yerha Park features Cary's outdoor Pickleball courts" and "Three pickleball courts", and records the renaming for a councilmember who served 2012 to 2022. sources.publisher: Town of Wake Forest, Parks, Recreation & Cultural Resources
sources.evidence: "Pickleball began in Wake Forest in 2009 on one chalked tennis court. Today, the sport has grown to include three shared use (basketball, volleyball, tennis) indoor courts at Flaherty Park Community Center, three shared use indoor courts at Joyner Park Community Center, eight shared use outdoor courts at Flaherty Park Tennis Courts, and four dedicated outdoor courts at Flaherty Park." "Since 2013 the Town has installed a total of 32 courts, including both shared use and dedicated courts. Wake Forest currently offers 18 shared use and/or dedicated active courts at Town-owned facilities." Dated timeline: 2013 approached by citizens asking for lines taped on a gym floor; 2014 resurfaced Flaherty Park Tennis Courts adding eight shared-use courts, and installed four at WF Middle School, "These courts are no longer in use"; 2015 resurfaced Heritage High School tennis courts with six shared-use courts, "Removal of these courts was requested once the dedicated court was installed", and partnered with SEBTS for temporary gym courts; 2016 added three courts to the new Flaherty Park Community Center gym floor; 2017 "Town unveiled the Flaherty Park Pickleball Courts which include four outdoor, lighted courts"; 2019 installed three at Joyner Park Community Center; 2021 approached about building a pickleball complex; 2022 "$24.4 million parks and recreation bond referendum passes which includes Multipurpose Sports Complex to house dedicated pickleball courts".

Two tables. The first lists twelve parks with columns Park, Number of Tennis Courts, Number of Lighted Tennis Courts, 10 & Under Lines, 8 & Under Lines, Pickleball Lines; Bethesda Park, Forest Hills Park, Garrett Road Park and Morreene Road Park read Yes under Pickleball Lines, with no pickleball court count given. The second table, headed Pickleball Court Information, contains a single row: Piney Wood Park, Number of Pickleball Courts 12, Number of Lighted Courts 12.

sources.publisher: Town of Holly Springs, Parks & Recreation
sources.evidence: "The four outdoor pickleball courts at North Main Athletic Complex (NMAC) are available on a first-come, first-served basis at no charge." Indoor pickleball open play runs at the W.E. Hunt Center on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, 11:15 a.m. to 1:15 p.m., with "Up to three nets are available"; open play passes are $2 for residents and $3 for non-residents. Court lighting is activated by a button on the light pole for an hour at a time, with a strobe roughly six minutes before shutoff.

sources.publisher: City of Raleigh Parks, Recreation and Cultural Resources
sources.evidence: "Lighting upgrades continue on the pickleball courts at North Hills Park." Work began 24 August 2026 with completion targeted for 8 September 2026; daytime play resumed 2 September 2026 with night play closed until the work finishes. Separately, the Baileywick court closure notice posted 24 August 2026 states "Due to repairs, Baileywick Park Pavilion-Court A is currently closed" with no reopening date. Baileywick's park page lists Court A as Covered and Court B as Covered Center and schedules pickleball on Courts A and B; Raleigh's pickleball page gives the park 6 courts while the city's GIS Athletic Courts layer totals 4.

County resolved individually for all nineteen verified North Carolina venues; all return Wake County, FIPS 37183. Resolution is per venue rather than per town because a TIGERweb intersect of the Apex town polygon against Census county boundaries returns two counties, Wake and Chatham, and Raleigh extends into Durham County at Brier Creek. The ZCTA-to-county file shows both Apex postcodes, 27502 and 27523, spanning Wake and Chatham.
